(43) In the *yājyā*s ending with *iṅgya*, in the stationary, and in one's own, [the rule] "not" (*na*) applies; in the subsequent *sana*, all are *āsate*; in the preceding, when clear, the subsequent [rule] applies in the *save*. (44)
It should be recited for Saṅgin, Sahasra, Sātaya, Stubha, Sūnu, Savana, Stoma, and likewise for Pūrva and Svasti;
and it should be employed for Sṛjanta, Savitṛ, and Pavamāna when the hymn is being praised.

Some [offerings] would first be for the unimpaired; likewise, we shall sprinkle for stability (sthiti), for the grain-crop (sasya), for Sinīvālī, for birth (sūti), for the spreading (stṛti), for creation (sṛṣṭi), and for prosperity (samṛddhi).
They are offered when called; I invoke [the one] beyond "neti. 46–47.

When the oblation has been offered into the Āhavanīya fire, we call upon the Hotṛ; when it is held in the hand, they carry it to the end without wavering; he calls out, he offers, for the sake of killing, to kill, and we shall carry [the offering].
48. It is abandoned, it is invoked, for the purpose of striking, to strike, and we shall take away.
"We invoke the *hari* for the sake of success; indeed, there are more [syllables] than these. (49) Thus ends the section on *vilaṅghya*.
Section 2: *napara*.
Now begins the section on the *napara*:
Having bowed to the supreme god Nārāyaṇa, the bestower of all prosperity, the son of Śauri shall proclaim this new, most excellent *napara*. 1.
That which is difficult to understand, difficult to recite, dependent on other works, or lacking in proper sequence—
having abandoned such [texts] along with their commentaries, this work, beginning with the letter 'A' and being complete,
need not be commenced, for it is established by its own nature.
Because its study is well-established, some have doubts in certain places;
yet by some skillful and great-souled ones,
it is determined and ascertained through characteristics corresponding to its own nature.
At the beginning, it is not subject to modification; *na* and *ta* at the end of a word are its scope.
Those two alone are the denotables, and the knowledge thereof is the purpose. [This applies] when *ca*, *cha*, or *ja* are followed by a dental (*tavargīya*) other than *tha*.
When the four [consonants] and the letter *m* are followed by the letter *l*,
and when the final *t* of a word is not followed by an *n*, I shall explain those words in which these [rules] are observed. (6–7)

In this grammatical definition, that which ends in an *iṅ* vowel is desired to consist of multiple syllables; whereas that which has a short vowel as its penultimate letter and does not end in an *iṅ* vowel is considered to have a single syllable (*tapara*). Examples include:
*nāgamam*, *śakeyam*, *acāriṣam*, and *aśakam*.
The six-word phrase "śrayadhvam enam" is prescribed.
The first word ends in *n*, and then, in sequence, those beginning with *a* and ending in *t* are taken according to this very order. 10.
Thus, according to this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*),
in that [context] they did not speak; in this [context], they became oxen (*anaḍvān*), they were Asuras, they dwelt, they performed labor, they led, and likewise they milked.
They milked it, they kindled it, they purchased it, they entered it,
they sought to win it, they blew upon it, they became it, and they brought it. They attained it, they taught it, they spoke it, they were not angry with it, they became it, and they carried it.
They entered it while it was not yet born; they stepped upon it while it was not yet formed; they perceived it while it was still invisible (3).
They caused it to enter, they sang it, and they found it as it was being grasped; they failed to reach it, they seized it, and they won it even while they did not know it (4).
He did not see anything beyond this, nor was anything else prohibited;
for there would have been nothing prior to this. O Long-lived One, even though he did not succeed, he then [perceived] the Ātman, as well as the Aśvattha tree and the Ādityas.

If he intends to go to the forest-dwellers, they should perform [the rites] without desiring to act; these [rites] are to be performed for those who desire to reach the world of the gods, which is to be praised and extolled. In this very [world], one should impel them toward the higher world of the gods.

Then, having impelled these and others such as the *airayas*, the *omanas*, the *kapālas*, the *krayaṇas*, the *kalpas*, the *garutmants*, the houses, and the courtyards— seizing the *valgās* like one who is compassionate, he became possessed of sight and thus made them complete.
"Having gone to Carmaṃ and Mañja, knowing, producing, and even while producing; 9.
let them stand near you, O powerful one; let those who are advancing stand near you, O Pan;
in that regard, the word 'iti' is clearly intended here as a marker. 10.
The *chandas* and the gods—these two [categories] from the right are not omitted in these [verses]; one should avoid those [verses] that one intends to recite among the subsequent ones.
11. One should consecrate oneself with the gods and the *daṇḍyus*, even while maintaining the portions.

Beholding in his flight the archers who drink Soma, the holy ones of the earth, the sinful, the devourers, the sacrificial cakes, the animals, and the Pitṛs; and seeing the Brahmins, the auspicious lights shining like blazing fires—he is called Bhūyāni. 12–13.
He who, though great, releases the Bhrātṛvyas, the Manasvins, the Maṇḍūkas, the Mrocas, the Malimluc-s, and the Maruts; he who is full of sweetness,
yet also [releases] humans, and in whom [he] shines, leading them by his footstep.
O King, those departing and those yet to come are called "heaven" (diva).
The travelers found the worlds from Rudra; the wise one obtained the ancient boons, as well as the Vasus, the Vāras, the heroes, and even the followers of Varuṇa upon the high ground. 15–16.
The word *vāniṅgyāntam* and the plural *viśvān* followed by *devān* are called *param*;
likewise, *śatrūñcharmachruśruvām* and *śīrṣandaparam* are desired [as such].
17. *Sāmanthsudhānthsarasvān* and *niṣīdanth sūryaḥ*, being present [in this manner], are [treated as *param*].
"Being present, you shall arise, surely crushing all serpents;
[you shall overcome] the obstacles along with the powerful ones through oblations with clarified butter—this is the method.
(18–19) Thus ends the third section on the *Napa*.
The Section on *ta*-following *p* (tapara-prakaraṇam):
Now begins the section on *ta*-following *p*.
[The forms] *adyāt*, *atṛṇat*, *aśnīyāt*, *abravīt*, and *ajuṣat* follow from that.
"asthāt" (he stood), "asmat" (from us), and "asat" (non-existent)—these likewise do not cause pride in other people.
"asmāt" (from this), "avasṛjet" (he would release), "avakramīt" (he stepped down), and "avastāt" (from below)—these are counted as such.
"abhavat" (it became), "avarohet" (he would descend), and "anamadāsīt" (he bowed)—this is so stated. 2.
After *iyāt* and above, these [rules] are not intended to apply further; likewise, after *svāhā* and from a single [word], when followed by a word ending in *i*,
one should perform this [elision] in the *pada* text, as in *krāmet*, *kanikradat*, and *khṣayāt*.
One should take it up, cause it to go forth, and offer it;
thus it has been described. One should not let it fall from that state, nor should one release it toward others who are not fit vessels. 4–5.
In the phrase "akurvatat," a negation is not desired; [the forms] didyu, daridru, dadhyāt, dheya,
naśat, hi, īritam, pātra— after these or before them— one should utter the word *pad*, as well as *bṛhat*.

From the *bhadrāt* [verse], and from the middle, a woman is desired from the *mithuna* [verse]. Whatever has been declared up to the *yajña* [verse] should be observed in this manner; one should avoid it.
From the *vapām* [verse], the portion is the *adṛṃhaṇā*; one should sow from the eastern world and recite [the verse].
From Vṛtra, from Vaiśvānara, and from the act of cutting (vraścana)—thus it is said;
he has sat down (āsīt), he shall sit (syāt), he has harmed (ahiṃsīt), and he shall harm (hiṃsyāt).
9. The former nidhana is *haviṣmat*, and likewise the nidhana is *haviṣkṛt*.
It should destroy the fatigue of others; thus has this *pada* been proclaimed.

This garland of *pada*s, ending in the letter *ta*, possessing nine jewels as its final syllables, and endowed with excellent qualities, has been composed by the knower of the Vedas as an ornament for the neck. 10–11.
Thus ends the section on *tapara*. Now begins the section on *avarṇi*.

Having set aside what is unspoken, what is obscured, what is excessively redundant, and what is ill-reputed, and having observed the sequence of letters beginning with *ka*, I shall compose this excellent treatise (*suvṛtti*) with clearly articulated speech according to the order of the phonemes.
[Now follows: "The letter *o* [is used] when covered by a preceding vowel, occurring at the beginning of a word within a *saṃhitā*."
This treatise is composed by us in order to understand the unvoiced (avarṇa). That which is not acute (udātta) in the word-text (padapāṭha) becomes acute upon the arrival of saṃhitā;
and that which is acute in the word-text becomes circumflex (svarita) upon the arrival of saṃhitā.
The vowel *o* that precedes a voiceless consonant (*aghoṣa*), as well as the *o* in a *saṃhitā* (euphonic junction),
and the *a* that follows those [vowels] at the beginning of a word in the *Padapāṭha*— these [become *av*].
However, this does not apply to a *repha* (*r*) situated at the beginning of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) when it is followed by the letter *cha*.
The vowel *a* that precedes these— namely, a conjunct consonant and so forth, the syllable *ya*, a word-initial *svarita*, and the *anusvāra*— is [treated as] at the beginning of a word.
The *śruti* (euphonic modification) of the Aśvinas consists of eight syllables, beginning with *asu-ra-akṣara-agni-agra*, which have the middle *udātta* accent.
The words *araṇya* and *aruṇa* do not end in the vowel *u*; the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) [uses] *aditi*.
The word *aśva* does not end in *vi* or *chv*; the word *amṛta* does not end in *y* or *t*.
However, when preceded by *na*, as in *nakṛntata*, the letter *ā* is not found there.
The word *adhvaryu* and these others are preceded by the vowel *a* according to the Vedic text itself.
Whatever word belonging to the opponent's position occurs in the passage "yadyaddadāta," one should omit all such words beginning with *a* for the sake of generating [the mantra].
They did not perform the *upasarga* with *ṅ*, nor that preceded by *y*; they did not do it for *akarat*, *akrān*, or *akurvata*, nor for *akūpārasya*.
They did not perform it for *akurvan*, nor for *akarṇā uttaraṃ tathā*.
They did not desire it for *akramiṣam*, nor did he desire it for *akāmayata*, nor did he perform it for *akāram*.
The western region, where crops ripen without being ploughed, they have stepped upon; they have eaten there both crosswise and straight.
From the two eyes, they have gone to what is not heavy, and they have gone neither to the further nor the nearer shore.
They are those who do not go, yet they have come; I have gone, and we, ungrasped, have gone.
He seized, he sang, he struck, he went, and he also poured;
there might be one who acts as a restrainer (*avagraha*) against sin (*agha*); likewise, he moved and he cut. 13.
There may be a sacrifice performed by one whose [sacrificial post] was being cut; he was born, he sacrificed, and he would conquer in milk.
Those who were unborn and he who was unborn did not depart with a raised end;
likewise, the Unborn begat those who were born, and the Eternal also begat them.
If preceded by *yudh*, it does not take the suffix *aṇ*; even in the opinion of Atri, it is not so.
He stood here from Atīkāśa; from the waters came the Ādri, and through the waters he took, and thus he established it.
He who is unassailable and toothless, he gave that which was to be given, that which is invincible, and that which is to be eaten, as it was given.
16. He gave what was to be given, the invincible; he ate that which was given.
He gave, he rose up, he held fast, he milked; 17.
He desired to give, he also ate, he placed, he bestowed, he established—thus he deposited seed for me, it was deposited by me below, even crosswise. 18.

*Krandana*, *animiṣa*, *anāpta*, and *anamitra* mean "one who cries out," "one who does not blink," "one who has not attained," and "one who is not a friend" respectively; likewise, *anaktu* is stated to mean "one who anoints," while *anaśan* is also proclaimed [to have a similar sense].
*Anīka* means "without a face," *anāyatana* means "without a dwelling," and *anaḍvāh* means "one who does not carry a burden. 19. *Anṛta* means "untruth."
The word *anu* is followed by an udātta accent; likewise, there are *anvak* and *anovāhau*. In these two cases, there is no avagraha. There are *anaḍvān*, *anirdiṣṭā*, *anapāḥ*, and *apathāt*.
Also *apibat*, *apatat*, *aprāḥ*, and similarly *apaḥ* with an udātta at the end. (20–21)
Having not reached the *aponaptrīya* [offering], he saw water in his sleep; having not obtained water, he saw it with two others.
He did not spread out with water, he fell away, he gratified, he afflicted, and he also feared.
He spoke and he bore; they also spoke, they became, and they approached.
23 Having gone forth toward the portions, they were; one after another they brought, he brought, and he became; he overcame the adversary and he existed on all sides. 24

He meditated upon non-existence, and he was non-existent; he practiced, and he was unable to do so; he was like that, and he was not like that; he thought of him, and likewise his enemies were in him;
he did not become deluded, and from him, in her, and even among his ministers. 25.
They thought, "For this [purpose], we shall offer an oblation consisting of impure things.
Even with a lack of faith, they sacrificed for the sake of a firm pillar of iron and for the sake of a path;
they went toward that which is not elevated, free from disease, and they caused [him] to sacrifice and they went.

"Disjoined," "not ending in *svāra*," "not joined," and "for ten thousand"—these are used in the three [verses] beginning with "the unimpaired, for the unimpaired, may he sacrifice the iron [vessel]. "The sacrifice that does not proceed" or "excessive ground. 28. [End of section].
"Ransomed, he is born; may that darkness depart from our offspring through you.
[The verse continues: "Called upon by the king, rejoicing, like a king, do not abandon me;
go, he gathers [the wealth], svāhā!"—this [formula] follows after these [verses]. 29–30.

Therefore, one should desire the supreme; yet one should not hate, for this one does not first act as an enemy toward those who are not enemies— toward the non-hostile, the foe, the one who intends harm,
the one who causes injury, the one who is hostile, the one who has ascended to enmity, and even toward those who are dustless (pure).
Likewise, those who mount the chariot of delight, even though they are hairless, obtained abundance;
likewise, they have obtained it, they shall protect, they do protect, and they have protected—the fierce ones who are free from cruelty. 32–33.
The ignorant one has slain me, and though not being released, you have spoken;
he has carried away and has also protected from the wells; he found and he covered and he encompassed.
34 Indra has protected, he has chosen, he has obtained, and even with the lowest ones he has turned back the distress.
Seeking protection through his own power of aid, he protects both the present and the future;
35 The goats and sheep, though they are not to be warded off, have descended into the pits;
they have cleared away the obstacles, they have eaten the fodder, and the sheep have moved about and dwelt there. 36

And from those who were not to be rained upon, he struck back with the western [missile] on the day of non-rain; he pierced them with the *aviravāka* weapon, being himself unperturbed, protected by the *avṛka* [non-wolfish] ones.
Thus he made them more submissive, and he caused them to lie down for the sake of subjection.
He created the eighty Aṣāḍhās, which are like the teeth of a boar;
thus he was non-existent, elevated, non-existent, dark, and a striker.
He leaped up together with the seat, and he, the one who causes to settle, settled upon this. 38–39.
They cast [it] away; they praised it; it stood firm; it stood for us; it has come to rest; it exists for him; it has remained for him; it sat down; it was struck down within her, but not by us. 40.
The serpent, the slayer of Ahi, the devourer of the oblation, has slain the eater of the oblation; he has taken away the day.
"I took," "I am taking," "I have taken," "I was taken," "I shall take," and "I have been taken"—this is stated as the summary of the short [vowels].
(41) Thus ends the section on the letter *a* (avarṇi). 5.

Now begins the section on the *āvarjana* (turning away). Regarding the *āgnīdhra*, the *āgrayaṇa*, the clarified butter (*ājya*), and the *upāvarta*, there is the scriptural statement concerning the weapons (*āyudha*).
The Vedic texts concerning the Āśīr, the Āhavanīya fire, the Āgneya sacrifice, and the Agnāmuṣyāyaṇa;

the word *ātman* when not preceded by *uraḥ* or similar terms; the word *āyus* when not followed by *agha*; and the word *āditya* when it has an udātta accent on the final syllable or is unaccented—these are accepted as designations for the Sun.

the Śruti speaks of these two as the receptacles for the oblation, and their names are not derived from anything else.
One should perform the *upākaraṇa* (dedication) and other rites, and one performs them for that which has been prepared (*ākṛta*).
In the *iṣṭi* sacrifices, when one performs them out of season through intention (*ākūti*), that intention becomes the *ākṛta*.
Likewise, there is the act of crying out (*ākrandayata*), the act of attacking (*ākramya*), and even the act of stepping forward (*ākramaṇa*).
Thus, for the sake of intention (*ākūtāya*) and through the act (*ākṛtyā*), the *kūta* came to the *ākhara*.
He approaches the Āgnimāruta [offering], and then he approaches the iṅgya;
having approached, he is most ready to come, and then he should offer the Āghāra libation.
He should offer the Āghāra while moving, and then the piled-up [oblation] and the race.
May he anoint with the two testicles; may he prepare the guest-offering and protect against heat.

May he protect from the heat, may he protect from the sun, may he protect the one who exerts himself, by means of what causes trembling, may he protect from the heat, may he protect from the sun, may he protect the one who has attained it, and may he protect from the sun.

The first [group] begins with *ādāya* (having taken), and likewise *ādahana* (burning); then there are *ādāna* (taking), *adhimādhīta* (intensely studied), *ādhipatya* (sovereignty), and *ādhayaḥ* (mental anxieties).
There is also *ādhāna* (placing/impregnation) and *āntyāyana* (the final course), as well as *ānujāvara* (younger brother).
They sang the Ānṛcu and the Anuṣṭubh-vāk; likewise they obtained the bow and then the waters (āpsīḥ).
For the sake of attainment (āptyai), having attained (āptvā), and likewise the attained (āptā) and the waters (āpaḥ), ending with the Svāra.
Beholding the western (āpaḥ), the one who causes to obtain (āpayitā), and the one who has fled (apalāyitāya), [he gave] the answer (uttaram). 10–11.
By means of the *yajuṣ*, one attains [it] from these and by these; it is not [derived] from the *avagraha*.
There may be *āmbānām* and *āmanaṃ*, as well as *āmamat* for one afflicted with disease (*āmayāvin*).
(12) By means of *āmikṣā*, one causes disease to cease; likewise, they approach *āyuḥ* and *āyatīm*.

In the case of these [mantras], such as "sitāya," "sūryaḥ," and "pṛthivyāḥ," the vowel *ā* is not elided;

likewise, *āvavarti*, *āvyādha*, *āviṣṭitam*, and *āśiram*.

Salutations to the one who is devoid of the three qualities (guṇas), the creator of the three worlds, the eternal witness of the three Vedas, and the destroyer of the three cities (Tripura). Having paid homage to the remover of obstacles, this instruction is imparted.

A word that is a locus of doubt due to its similarity to both unmovable and movable things; a word designated by the sounds *śru* or *śruc*; a word that is modified by being composed of non-word elements;

By means of the [suffixes] *bhis*, *bhyām*, *bhyas*, and *su*, having permanently abandoned the state of being "cow" (*go*)— whether short or long— one does not waver; for by the hearing of the word *bhis* in "cow" (*go*), "singer" (*gī*), and "celestial drum" (*suradundu*),
everything preceding it likewise becomes *su* through the initial syllables.

The words beginning with *vaikāra*, *vaiṣṇa*, *vaiśvāyuksāsaha*, and so forth; those beginning with *saukāra*, *saparyā*, *nīya-vīya-āmaya*, and so forth; and those beginning with *traikāra* and *kukāra*, excluding those joined with *na-so-gopa-ī*. 6–7.

If the first syllable is short (i), and the word is situated between single consonants, then *arāti* and so forth, *vāvādi*, those ending in *jaś* sounds, *prathādi*, *dhūrvātiṣṭhādi*, *paṣṭhau*, *turyau*, *dityau*, and *vyathādi* [are examples].

The words *nīpya*, *āyudha*, *āśava*, *āsīna*, *avaṭya*, *āvārya*, and so forth; likewise, *īṅkāra* and others; *īmavāpa*, *upasannyut*, *dviprāyugya*; that *śruti* [is used] in the sense of "snorting" (*prothate*) and in the sense of "upward" (*ūrdhve*); [the suffix] *-pakṣe* with *datvat* and others; beginning with *adādi*; and for the meanings "one who has abandoned semen" (*aretaskāya*) and "one who is breathless" (*aprāṇate*). 13.

Now, [the hymn]: "O Anamitra, O Anyatarambarīṣa, we have heard; may Aśvatara slay the blameless one. May the two who have teeth for biting protect the unassailable one with their speech. 1.
You two vied with each other; you were seized by the pathless one, yet you both listened and practiced, O sinless ones who drink from the gods.
You reached the *apsarases* of the one who listens, the watchful ones, flowing along the river that is not coarse.
The word "taken away" (*avatta*) is not cattle; it is not fit for cattle, O listener, for the horse shone forth as Apnavāna.

Falling from within, impure, reaching the further shore, following the island, and not looking around; established by the Anuṣṭubh, unscattered, without bricks, for blessings, for the sake of blessing, fearless, not fleeing, for attainment; sinless, invincible, guiltless, heard from afar, free from evil, free from blemish—other than the thumb. 4.
The goat, the one with a pale appearance, the calf, the beloved, the offered, the bull, the hornless one, the one not neighing, the one not bellowing, the draught-ox— having heard these,
the python, through its fault, becomes devoid of intelligence; may it become devoid of offspring.

May the ocean be without cattle, may it be without blessings for others; may the pit be without a bottom, and may the cake be without a hole. May the pits be dustless, the wolves be without mouths, and may those who listen be free from disease.
The Atharvans, renowned as guests, [overcome] one who does not harm, who does not press the soma, who does not give, who does not ask, who is without a barrier, and who is irresistible—
[overcoming] even the most intimate [enemy] through the Adhvaryu rites, with the word for iron and the word for disease.
The Adhvaryu priest, hearing [the call], like one who has looked upon the dark [sacrificial fire], [is present] with the imperishable [verses];
may he, the lowest, protect the non-sacrificer from the low;
may he reach the reins with his unerring [arrows] and bring them to rest.
The beloved, the one who bestows splendor upon others, the one who is not hungry among those who are hungry, the one who is not surrounded by enemies, the one who is not in a place of confinement,
the one who is not subject to the downward flow of breath, the protector, the tearless, the one who has struck down the small;
the self, the descendant of Muṣya, the lineage of Ṛṣi, the alms, the one pertaining to Agni, the impelling, the sacred revelation.
The raw vessel (āmāṇḍa) is the one who hears; the wild ones are the sun-like sounds. 12.

The one who has reached [the goal] is Jīgarti Mārta; the hearing of the distressed is for the one who has overcome distress; the hearing of the seasonal is for the Āpyas; the Aśvattha tree is the hearing of the Aśvins; you shall obtain the vessel of the mouth (āspātra). 13.
*Āvithātharvaṇaḥ*, *cākhaḥ*, *ākhurātitthyá-*, and *śabdávat*;

The eaters, the takers, and the consumers, for the sake of eating, O swift-moving one;

The non-injurers have moved forward; the one who causes to obtain has come for the living one, for the sake of the living one.
And the eater has eaten the milk-mixture, O Asura; from the enemy, the one famous for the Āgrayaṇa draught has taken it away.
Like a throne, the desire-granting, manifest Agni and Indra, the possessors of power, have entered.
The *iṣṭarga*, the *iṣṭakelān*, the *daśrudidāvathsara*, and the *īhenya*;

Having prepared the common portion together with the *sardigṛdhi* for the assembly and for the wild dogs and reptiles, and having combined the *svātta* and the sounds of thunder together in one place, there are the *saṅkā* offerings.
Then follow the *sāvitra*, *sāhantya*, *sapatna*, and *sūnṛtā* offerings, along with the sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) characterized by the sound of the plowshare (*halīkṣṇa*).
The *hotrīya* [cup] belongs to the winter season (*hemanta*), as does the *haimantika-śrut* [sacrificial vessel]; the *hika* is made of gold (*hiraṇmaya*).
(75) Because the manifold details of these indistinct [objects] would be endless, only a mere indication has been provided here;
therefore, whatever remains unmentioned should be inferred by the wise. (76)
This path of the *aniṅgya* words has been revealed by the Sugata,
the wise son of the Goddess, who bears the Śrīvatsa mark, for the followers of the Taittirīya school.
Thus ends the seventh section, the *Aniṅgyaprakaraṇa*.
The seven characteristics are completed.
